findings.claim: licences are contractual agreements, not a form of IP protection in themselves.
findings.truth: Spec 5.2.3 names licencing as one of the four methods of intellectual property protection for computer systems and software (copyright, patents, trademarks, licencing). The lesson body ('There are four types you need to know') and the conclusion both teach licencing as the fourth method, so the exam tip contradicts the spec and the lesson, and would stop a student writing a creditable answer.

findings.claim: It covers three categories of offence: ... and making unauthorised modifications to computer material
findings.truth: The Computer Misuse Act 1990 as amended now creates five offences: s1 unauthorised access, s2 unauthorised access with intent to commit a further offence, s3 unauthorised acts with intent to impair operation (substituted by the Police and Justice Act 2006, which replaced the original 'unauthorised modification' wording), s3ZA unauthorised acts causing serious damage (Serious Crime Act 2015) and s3A making, supplying or obtaining articles. Options: (a) leave the three-offence framing, which is the standard GCSE simplification and which this spec never contradicts because it names no legislation at all, and which the lesson already qualifies by describing the 2015 amendment; or (b) rewrite the paragraph to the current five offences, which adds detail beyond the spec and forces re-narration. Recommendation: (a), no edit.
findings.evidence: Computer Misuse Act 1990 as amended; spec Topic 5 names no Acts (grep for 'Act 19', 'Act 20' returns only the Equality Act 2010 in the access-arrangements section)
findings.ruling: NOTE: three-offence GCSE framing of the Computer Misuse Act kept; the spec names no legislation.

findings.claim: When an autonomous vehicle causes a collision while operating without a human driver ... the existing framework struggles to assign responsibility cleanly.
findings.truth: UK law is not silent here: the Automated and Electric Vehicles Act 2018 s2 makes the insurer directly liable for damage caused by an automated vehicle while it is driving itself in Great Britain. However s5 preserves the insurer's right of recovery against whoever is actually at fault, so the underlying question the lesson describes does remain open. The claim is defensible and the surrounding text already hedges ('contracts and insurance arrangements may allocate liability'). No edit.
findings.evidence: legislation.gov.uk, Automated and Electric Vehicles Act 2018 s2

findings.claim: [3] 'When an autonomous vehicle causes a collision without a human driver, existing legal frameworks struggle to assign _____ because they assume a human made the decision.' Options: accountability / liability / ownership / consent; correct = 1 (liability).
findings.truth: The marked answer is the better one ('legal frameworks' cues legal liability), but the lesson teaches accountability as its own named issue in the same lesson, so option 0 is also defensible and a student who picks it is marked wrong. Options: (a) leave it; (b) replace option 0 'accountability' with a clearly wrong term such as 'copyright' so only one answer works. Recommendation: (b).
findings.evidence: lesson 2 sections 'Issue 1: Accountability' and 'Issue 4: Legal Liability'
findings.ruling: 'accountability' distractor swapped for 'copyright' so only 'liability' fits.

findings.claim: Three forms appear in the specification. (phishing, pretexting, shouldering)
findings.truth: Spec 5.3.1 says only that hackers 'use social engineering to carry out cyberattacks'. It names no forms at all. Phishing, pretexting/blagging and shouldering are named by other boards, not by this one. Teaching them as examples is right; attributing them to the specification is not.
findings.evidence: spec lines 692-697 (5.3.1); grep for 'phishing', 'pretext', 'shoulder', 'blagging' returns zero hits in the spec

findings.claim: Five specific protection methods are named in the specification: anti-malware software, encryption, acceptable use policies, backup, and recovery procedures.
findings.truth: Spec 5.3.2 lists four comma-separated items: 'anti-malware, encryption, acceptable use policies, backup and recovery procedures'. The last item is one compound entry. Splitting it into five to teach is fine; saying the specification names five is not.
Residue of F6 in the Key Fact box: 'named' reads as named-by-the-specification. Change to 'The five protections to learn are:'.

findings.claim: the specification lists exactly five — anti-malware, encryption, acceptable use policies, backup and recovery procedures. Do not add others (firewalls, biometrics, two-factor authentication are not in this list).
findings.truth: Firewalls, access control and physical security are named in this same specification at 4.2.1 (network security), and penetration testing and ethical hacking at 4.2.1 too. Paper 1 assesses Topics 1 to 5 together, so a firewall is a creditable point in an answer about protecting an organisation's systems. Telling students not to write it makes them withhold marks. The count 'exactly five' is also wrong (see F6).
findings.evidence: spec lines 645-649 (4.2.1) and 698-700 (5.3.2); spec lines 243-246 (Paper 1 assesses Topics 1 to 5)

findings.claim: [10].q 'Name the five protections specified for defending digital systems.'
findings.truth: Last residue of the F6 claim. 'specified' reads as specification-named.

summary: Exam anchors, tariffs and answer keys are sound: every practice tariff sits inside the Paper 1 command-word taxonomy (Give/State/Name 1, Identify 1, Define 1-2, Describe 2-4, Explain 2-4, Discuss 6) and all 15 knowledge-check keys recompute correct. The errors are exam advice and spec attribution: lesson 1 tells students licencing is not a method of IP protection when spec 5.2.3 names it as one, and lesson 3 tells them not to mention firewalls when the same spec names firewalls at 4.2.1, plus two smaller mis-attributions of social-engineering forms and a protection count to the specification.
